newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany against zero land set-aside - Bonn official.
newsitem.headline: Germany against zero land set-aside - Bonn official.

text.p: Germany is opposed to proposals by other European Union member states to cut the rate for idled farm land for the 1998 harvest to zero, a Bonn government official said on Thursday.
"We need land set-aside because we have to comply with restrictions on the permissible grain export volume under GATT," said Hermann Engelhardt, head of grain in the Bonn agriculture ministry.
"If the rate was cut to zero, there would be little chance of reintroducing set-aside."

Engelhardt's comments were taken from remarks he prepared for delivery at a Bremen grain trade meeting, which he made available to Reuters. France, supported by some other EU states, has suggested a zero rate to keep exports flowing.
Regardless of his opposition, Engelhardt agreed with France that the set-aside issue must be settled early.
"It must be decided in June or July at the latest to allow farmers to plan ahead," he said.
Engelhardt added zero set-aside for the harvest next year would generate even more grain in an already well supplied market.
The record grain crop harvested in the EU in 1996 -- after the set-aside rate was reduced -- had not been disposed of and there were gaps in the balance, he said.
"Analysts expected 10-12 million tonnes of grain intervention in 96/97 but now a figure between two and 3.5 million tonnes looks more likely," he said.
"While more grain has gone into feeds, exports have also fallen short of earlier projections."
"We can only assume that consumer stocks have been rebuilt."
The EU expects an even higher crop this year after a further set-aside cut and due to grain area expansions by two to three percent.
